question: The Gospel Topics essay "First Vision Accounts" acknowledges that Joseph Smith left several differing recitals of the 1820 theophany. Which statement best represents the official Church position on why these accounts differ?
choices: The differences are consistent with Joseph emphasizing different aspects to different audiences over time—analogous to Paul's varied retellings of his Damascus-road experience—while the 1838 account (Joseph Smith—History) was canonized as scripture.
Joseph's story evolved over the years: his earliest accounts mention only Jesus or a forgiveness of sins, and he later added God the Father to strengthen the Church's doctrinal claims.
Because the accounts cannot be fully harmonized, the First Vision is best understood as an inward, subjective spiritual awakening rather than a literal appearance of divine beings.
Joseph personally recorded only the 1838 account; the so-called earlier accounts were composed by scribes without his knowledge or approval.
All of the accounts are word-for-word identical in their essentials, which is itself the strongest evidence of the vision's authenticity.
source: Gospel Topics Essay, "First Vision Accounts"; Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20
notes: Tests whether a model grasps the official reconciliation (complementary accounts for varied audiences, 1838 canonical) versus the CES-Letter 'evolving embellishment' spin (anti_mormon_trap) and the Sunstone 'subjective experience' reframe (progressive_trap). The near-miss falsely denies Joseph's authorship of the 1832 holograph; the oversimplification ('identical') contradicts the essay itself, which openly concedes the differences.

question: John the Baptist restored the Aaronic Priesthood on May 15, 1829. Regarding the restoration of the Melchizedek Priesthood by Peter, James, and John, what is the most accurate statement of the Church's position on its timing?
choices: It occurred on May 15, 1829, the same day John the Baptist conferred the Aaronic Priesthood.

The exact date was never recorded; it took place sometime after the Aaronic Priesthood restoration in 1829 (likely late May or early June), and the Church affirms the event without fixing a precise day.
Because no contemporaneous 1829 document describes it, the Melchizedek restoration was a narrative constructed and backdated years afterward.
It happened on April 6, 1830, the day the Church was organized, when the higher priesthood was first needed.
It was conferred on the same day and by the same heavenly messenger as the Aaronic Priesthood.
source: D&C 13 (heading); D&C 27:12–13; D&C 128:20; Gospel Topics, "Priesthood Restoration"
notes: Expert discriminator: the honest, defensible answer is that the precise date is unrecorded—a point Roberts and later Church historians acknowledge. The near-miss conflates it with the well-documented Aaronic date; the folk_doctrine_trap ties it to the organization date; the anti_mormon_trap weaponizes the documentary gap into a fabrication claim, which the Church rejects while still affirming the date is unknown.

question: A careful reading of the end of plural marriage requires distinguishing the 1890 Manifesto from later developments. Which statement most accurately describes how the practice actually wound down?
choices: The 1890 Manifesto immediately and completely ended all plural marriage among Latter-day Saints everywhere.

The 1890 Manifesto (OD-1) declared Wilford Woodruff's intent to submit to the law and stop new plural marriages, but some marriages continued—often performed outside the United States—until President Joseph F. Smith's 1904 Second Manifesto brought firm enforcement, including Church discipline of those who persisted.
The Second Manifesto was issued by Wilford Woodruff in 1904 as a clarification of his own earlier 1890 declaration.
The Manifesto was a deliberate public deception; Church leaders never intended to end polygamy and quietly sanctioned it indefinitely.
Plural marriage was abandoned solely for the political goal of statehood, with no claim of revelation, making OD-1 a secular policy rather than scripture.
source: Official Declaration 1 (1890); Gospel Topics Essay, "The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage"; Second Manifesto (1904, Joseph F. Smith)
notes: Tests synthesis the Sunday-School answer misses: the 1890 Manifesto did not instantly halt the practice, and full cessation required the 1904 Second Manifesto under Joseph F. Smith (with discipline of apostles Taylor and Cowley). The oversimplification is the correlated shorthand; the near-miss misattributes the Second Manifesto to Woodruff; the anti_mormon and progressive traps deny, respectively, the leaders' good faith and the revelatory basis the Church affirms.
